entities.name: Civic Opera House
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Civic Opera House in Chicago, opened in November 1929 — just weeks after the Black Tuesday stock market crash that inaugurated the Great Depression — is the second-largest opera house in North America (after the Metropolitan Opera in New York, which it was designed to rival) and an Art Deco masterpiece whose distinctive two-wing commercial building design (nicknamed 'Insull's Throne') reflects the extraordinary ambition and hubris of its builder, utility magnate Samuel Insull, who envisioned it as the center of Chicago's cultural life.

Architect Graham, Anderson, Probst & White designed the 3,563-seat opera house (now 3,563 seats) within a 45-story commercial office building — a radical commercial-cultural hybrid that made the opera house financially self-supporting through rental income from its offices. Insull — who founded Chicago's electric utilities and whose business empire collapsed spectacularly in 1932 (the largest corporate failure in US history up to that point) — spent approximately $20 million on the building in 1929 dollars. His financial collapse left Chicago without regular opera until the Lyric Opera of Chicago was founded in 1954.

The Civic Opera House is the home of the Lyric Opera of Chicago, founded in 1954 and ranked consistently as one of North America's three greatest opera companies. The building itself — with its Art Deco interiors, gold-leaf ceiling, and massive pipe organ — is considered one of Chicago's architectural treasures. Maria Callas's American debut at the Lyric Opera (1954) was one of opera history's defining moments; the Lyric subsequently became known as 'the house that Callas built.'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Civic Opera House — North America's second-largest opera house, built by the Great Depression's most spectacular corporate failure, and home to Maria Callas's American debut — is a symbol of American cultural ambition and the unexpected connections between business hubris and cultural achievement.
